title: A sigma-algebra as information
objectives: Read a sigma-algebra as what is known, using a coin-flip tree.

screens.title: What is still possible
screens.prose: Topic 3.2 is optional. It serves desk quant and derivatives pricing roles. A coin is tossed three times, and the grid lists the 8 outcomes. The first toss lands heads, and you see nothing else.
screens.question: Tap every outcome that is still possible.

hints.text: Which outcomes disagree with a heads on toss 1?
Every outcome that starts with T is gone.
Keep HHH, HHT, HTH and HTT.

feedback.correct: Four outcomes remain. Everything starting with T is ruled out.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep only the outcomes whose first toss is H.

byKey.two-heads: You kept the outcomes with at least two heads. Only the first toss is known, so the first letter decides.
byKey.all: You kept the whole grid. A heads on toss 1 rules out the four outcomes that start with T.
byKey.one: You kept only HHH. Tosses 2 and 3 are still open, so four outcomes remain.

explain.text: A first toss of H rules out the four outcomes that start with T. The four that remain are HHH, HHT, HTH and HTT. The first toss splits the grid into two groups, and you now know which group you are in.

screens.title: Events that are decided
screens.prose: After the first toss you know which of the two groups you are in. An event is **decided** when that knowledge answers yes or no.
screens.question: Select all that apply: which events are decided by the first toss?

options.text: The first toss is H
At least two heads in the three tosses
options.why: You asked whether the count is settled. A first H leaves HTT, with one head, and HHT, with two.

options.text: The third toss comes up tails
options.why: You looked at the last toss. After one toss it is still open.

options.text: Something happens: all of $\Omega$

hints.text: Can you say yes or no from the first toss alone?
Check each event against both groups.
Only the first toss and the sure event are decided.

feedback.correct: The first toss and the sure event. The other two split a group.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Test each event against both groups.

byKey.b: You checked the count of heads. The H group holds outcomes with one, two and three heads.
byKey.c: You used the third toss, which is not yet known.

explain.text: The first toss separates the groups, so it decides itself. The sure event $\Omega$ is decided too. At least two heads is true for HHH and false for HTT, and both are in the H group.

screens.title: Slide through time
screens.prose: Slide time forward. Cells with the same number are outcomes you cannot yet tell apart. Count the groups at time 2.
screens.question: How many groups are there once two tosses are seen?

hints.text: Set the slider to time 2.
Each group shares its first two tosses.
HH, HT, TH and TT make four.

feedback.correct: Four groups. Each pair of outcomes agrees on tosses 1 and 2.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Set time to 2 and count the colours.

byKey.two: That is the count at time 1. A second toss splits each group again.
byKey.eight: That is the count at time 3. At time 2 the third toss is still unknown, so outcomes pair up.
byKey.three: You gave 3, the number of values of $S_2$. The atoms of $\mathcal{F}_2$ are HH, HT, TH and TT.

explain.text: Each toss splits every group in two, so the groups go 1, 2, 4, 8. At time 2 the pairs HHH and HHT, and so on, are still merged. These groups are called atoms.

screens.title: Counting the events
screens.prose: Write $\mathcal{F}_n$ for the sigma-algebra the first $n$ tosses decide. Its **atoms** are the groups, and its events are every union of atoms. With $k$ atoms there are $2^k$ events.
screens.question: Fill in the atoms and the events at times 2 and 3.

hints.text: An event is any union of atoms, so each atom is in or out.
At time 2 there are 4 atoms, so 4 in-or-out choices.

feedback.correct: 16 events at time 2 and 256 at time 3. Each atom is either in an event or out.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the atoms first, then count the in-or-out choices.

byKey.r0c2: You gave the number of atoms. Every union of atoms is an event, so count the choices, $2^4$.
byKey.r1c2: You gave the number of atoms. Every union of atoms is an event, so count the choices, $2^8$.
byKey.r0c1: Each toss doubles the atoms. Two tosses give 4.
byKey.r1c1: Each toss doubles the atoms. Three tosses give 8.

explain.text: At time 2 each of the four atoms is in or out of an event, so $2^4 = 16$. At time 3 there are 8 atoms and $2^8 = 256$ events. Knowing more tosses grows the family of decided events very fast.

screens.title: Constant on atoms
screens.prose: A variable is $\mathcal{F}_2$-measurable when it is decided by two tosses. The grid shows $S_3$, the heads in all three tosses, under each outcome.
screens.question: Select all that apply: which variables are $\mathcal{F}_2$-measurable?

options.text: $S_2$, the heads in the first two tosses
$\mathbf{1}\{\text{the first two tosses match}\}$
$S_3$, the heads in all three tosses
options.why: You counted the third toss too. HHH and HHT are one atom but give $S_3 = 3$ and $2$.

options.text: $\mathbf{1}\{\text{the third toss is T}\}$
options.why: You used a toss that two tosses do not show. HHH and HHT share an atom and differ here.

hints.text: Is the variable constant on each coloured atom?
Look at the pair HHH and HHT: same atom.
Only variables built from the first two tosses are constant on all four atoms.

feedback.correct: $S_2$ and the match indicator are constant on every atom. $S_3$ and the third toss are not.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check whether the variable takes one value on each atom.

byKey.c: You added a third toss. A variable that changes inside an atom is not measurable for it.
byKey.d: The third toss changes inside every atom, so two tosses cannot decide it.

explain.text: A variable is $\mathcal{F}_n$-measurable exactly when it is constant on each atom of $\mathcal{F}_n$. $S_2$ and the match indicator pass. $S_3$ and the third toss change inside an atom, so they fail.

screens.title: What a count knows
screens.prose: Now keep only $S_3$. The atoms of $\sigma(S_3)$ group outcomes by their count: sizes 1, 3, 3 and 1, so $\sigma(S_3)$ has $2^4 = 16$ events.
screens.question: Which event is in $\sigma(S_3)$?

options.text: At least two heads
The first toss is H
options.why: You treated the count as the path. HHT and THH both give $S_3 = 2$, but only one starts with H.

options.text: The outcome is HHT
options.why: You picked out one path. HHT shares its count with HTH and THH, so $S_3$ cannot isolate it.

options.text: The second toss is H
options.why: You picked one position. The count does not say which toss gave the head.

hints.text: An event is in $\sigma(S_3)$ if it is a union of whole count-atoms.
The 2-head and 3-head atoms together hold 4 outcomes.
Only the count-based event is a union of whole atoms.

feedback.correct: At least two heads is the union of the 2-head and 3-head atoms.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The event must be a union of whole atoms of the count.

byKey.b: You assumed the count names the path. The 2-head atom has HHT, HTH and THH, which split on the first toss.
byKey.c: You tried to isolate a path. A count atom cannot be cut into its outcomes.

explain.text: The count atoms are $\{TTT\}$, the three one-head paths, the three two-head paths and $\{HHH\}$. Only unions of these are decided by $S_3$. The first toss splits the two-head atom, so it is not decided.

screens.title: Strictly inside
screens.prose: Now $S_2$, the heads in the first two tosses. It takes three values, so $\sigma(S_2)$ has the three atoms shown, with the pairs HT and TH merged.
screens.question: How many events are in $\sigma(S_2)$?

hints.text: Count the atoms first.
There are three atoms: two heads, one head, no heads.

feedback.correct: Eight events, from three atoms. That is fewer than the 16 of $\mathcal{F}_2$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the atoms of $\sigma(S_2)$ and take a power of 2.

byKey.f2: You gave the 16 events of $\mathcal{F}_2$. $S_2$ merges HT with TH, so it has only three atoms.
byKey.atoms: You gave the number of atoms. Each union of atoms is an event, so use $2^3$.
byKey.four: You gave the 4 atoms of $\mathcal{F}_2$. $S_2$ merges HT with TH into one atom, leaving three.

explain.text: $S_2$ has three atoms, so $\sigma(S_2)$ has $2^3 = 8$ events. That is a strict part of the 16 events of $\mathcal{F}_2$. Knowing the count is less than knowing the path.

screens.title: A count names the path
screens.prose: A colleague says: learning $S_2 = 1$ tells me which toss was heads. So $\sigma(S_2)$ is all of $\mathcal{F}_2$.
screens.question: Is $\sigma(S_2) = \mathcal{F}_2$?

options.text: No: HT and TH both give $S_2 = 1$
Yes: $S_2 = 1$ says which toss was heads
options.why: You assumed a count names the path. HT and TH have the same count, so $S_2$ cannot split them.

options.text: Yes: $S_2$ reads both of the tosses
options.why: You counted the tosses it reads. A variable can read two tosses and still merge their paths.

options.text: No: $S_2$ ignores the second toss
options.why: You dropped a toss. $S_2$ changes from 1 to 2 when toss 2 is H after an H.

hints.text: Find two outcomes with the same $S_2$ and different paths.
HT and TH both have one head.
They sit in one atom of $\sigma(S_2)$, so it is smaller than $\mathcal{F}_2$.

feedback.correct: HT and TH share the value 1, so they stay merged in one atom.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look for two different paths with the same count.

byKey.b: You read the count as a path. Two tosses with one head could be HT or TH, and $S_2$ cannot tell which.
byKey.c: Reading two tosses is not enough. What matters is whether different paths give different values.

explain.text: The event that the first toss is H is in $\mathcal{F}_2$, but it is not in $\sigma(S_2)$. It would have to separate HT from TH, and $S_2$ gives both the value 1. A function of the paths forgets whatever it merges.

screens.title: Atoms in code
screens.prose: On a finite space, a sigma-algebra is fixed by its atoms. Write `atoms(outcomes, X)`, which groups outcomes by the value of `X`, then `n_events` and `is_measurable`.
screens.question: Complete the three functions.

widget.prelude:
from itertools import product
OUT3 = [''.join(p) for p in product('HT', repeat=3)]
heads = lambda w: w.count('H')
first2 = lambda w: w[:2]

tests.call: [len(g) for g in atoms(OUT3, lambda w: w == 'HHH')]

widget.how: Check runs 11 hidden tests on the 8 outcomes of three tosses. `OUT3`, `heads` and `first2` are already defined for you.

hints.text: Build a dictionary from the value of `X` to the list of outcomes.
Sort the dictionary keys so the groups come in order of value.
`is_measurable` asks whether each atom has one value of `Y`.

feedback.correct: All 11 tests pass. The functions agree with the counts on the grid.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the order of the groups and the set of values on each atom.

explain.text: `atoms` groups outcomes by the value of `X`, ordered by value. `n_events` is $2^k$ for $k$ atoms. `is_measurable` checks that `Y` is constant on every atom, which is the test of the earlier screens.

screens.title: A lookback payoff
screens.prose: On the trees course's two-step tree, $S_0 = £100$, $u = 1.2$ and $d = 0.8$. The paths UD and DU both end at £96. A lookback call pays $\max(M - 100, 0)$, where $M$ is the running maximum, starting from $S_0$.
screens.question: Fill in the running maximum on each path.

hints.text: The running maximum includes the price at time 0.
DU goes 100, 80, 96, so its maximum is the start.

feedback.correct: £120 on UD and £100 on DU, though both end at £96.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. List the prices along each path and take the largest.

byKey.r0c2: You gave the final price. The maximum is the highest price on the way, 120 after the up move.
byKey.r1c2: You gave the final price. The path DU never rises above its start of 100.

explain.text: On UD the prices are 100, 120 and 96, so the maximum is £120. On DU they are 100, 80 and 96, so it is £100. The two paths have one final price and two maxima.

screens.title: History, not just the price
screens.prose: The lookback payoff is decided by two steps, so it is $\mathcal{F}_2$-measurable. It takes the values £20 and £0 on UD and DU, though both final prices are £96.
screens.question: Is it $\sigma(S_2)$-measurable, and what does a pricer need?

options.text: No: it needs the whole path, so $\mathcal{F}_2$
Yes: both paths end at £96, so the price decides it
options.why: You compared the final prices. UD and DU share one, yet their maxima and payoffs differ.

options.text: Yes: the up move is the same, so it is $\mathcal{F}_1$
options.why: You looked at the first move only. After U the next step still changes the payoff.

options.text: No: a payoff is never measurable for the price
options.why: A payoff on the final price alone is. Only the path-dependent part fails.

hints.text: Find two outcomes with the same $S_2$ and different payoffs.
UD and DU both give £96.
A $\sigma(S_2)$-measurable payoff cannot tell them apart.

feedback.correct: The payoff differs on two paths that $S_2$ merges, so it is not $\sigma(S_2)$-measurable.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Test whether the payoff is constant on each atom of $\sigma(S_2)$.

byKey.b: You assumed one final price means one payoff. Path-dependent options break that.
byKey.c: You assumed the first move decides. Both U and D start paths that split again.

explain.text: The atom $\{UD, DU\}$ of $\sigma(S_2)$ holds paths with different payoffs, so the lookback payoff is not constant on it. A path-dependent option needs the history, which is $\mathcal{F}_2$, not just the final price.

ideas: After $n$ tosses, $\mathcal{F}_n$ holds the events those tosses decide. Its atoms are the groups of outcomes you cannot tell apart.
With $k$ atoms there are $2^k$ events. A variable is measurable exactly when it is constant on every atom.
A function of the path forgets what it merges: $\sigma(S_2)$ is strictly smaller than $\mathcal{F}_2$.

formula.name: Information after n tosses
formula.note: Further reading: Williams, chapter 9; Shreve, Stochastic Calculus for Finance I, chapter 2.

summary.trap: A count does not name the path. Paths with equal counts stay merged in one atom.

quiz.prose: Suppose you know nothing, so your sigma-algebra is $\{\varnothing, \Omega\}$.
quiz.question: Which variables are measurable for it?

options.text: Only the constants
Every variable
options.why: You treated knowing nothing as knowing everything. A variable that changes across outcomes needs information to decide it.

options.text: Only the indicator of $\Omega$ and of $\varnothing$
options.why: These are constants too, but they are not the only ones. Every constant is measurable.

feedback.correct: Only constants are constant on the single atom $\Omega$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. With one atom, a measurable variable has one value.

explain.text: The trivial sigma-algebra has the single atom $\Omega$. A variable constant on it is a constant. Knowing nothing decides nothing that varies.

quiz.prose: Five tosses are made, and $\mathcal{F}_4$ is decided by the first four.
quiz.question: How many events are in $\mathcal{F}_4$?

feedback.correct: $2^{16} = 65{,}536$. There are 16 atoms, each in or out.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the atoms, then take a power of 2.

byKey.sixteen: You gave the number of atoms. Events are unions of atoms, so use $2^{16}$.
byKey.thirtytwo: You used the 32 outcomes. The atoms are the 16 groups of four tosses, merged over toss 5.
byKey.two5: You used all five tosses, which gives $2^{32}$. $\mathcal{F}_4$ has 16 atoms, so $2^{16}$ events.

explain.text: Four tosses give $2^4 = 16$ atoms, each holding two outcomes of five tosses. Every union of atoms is an event, so there are $2^{16} = 65{,}536$.

quiz.prose: Three tosses are made, and $Y$ counts the tails in the first two tosses.
quiz.question: Is $Y$ measurable for the sigma-algebra of the first toss alone?

options.text: No: $Y$ changes inside the atom H
Yes: it counts tails, and toss 1 can be a tail
options.why: You noticed that toss 1 contributes. $Y$ also depends on toss 2, which is unknown.

options.text: Yes: every count of tosses is measurable
options.why: You assumed counts are always decided. A count needs every toss it counts.

feedback.correct: After H, $Y$ is 0 or 1 depending on toss 2, so it is not constant on the atom.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check whether $Y$ is constant on the H atom.

explain.text: The atom H holds HH and HT, with $Y = 0$ and $1$. A variable that changes inside an atom is not measurable.

quiz.prose: Four tosses are made, and $S_4$ counts the heads.
quiz.question: How many events are in $\sigma(S_4)$?

feedback.correct: $S_4$ takes the values 0 to 4, so five atoms and $2^5 = 32$ events.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the values of $S_4$, then take a power of 2.

byKey.five: You gave the number of atoms. Count the unions, $2^5$.
byKey.sixteen: You used the 16 paths. $S_4$ merges paths with equal counts.
byKey.paths16: You used 16 paths in the exponent. $S_4$ has five atoms, so $2^5$.

explain.text: The values 0, 1, 2, 3 and 4 are five atoms with 1, 4, 6, 4 and 1 paths. Every union of atoms is an event, so there are $2^5 = 32$.
